report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **partially supported but overstated**. Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) supplementation produces, at best, a small and inconsistent reduction in body/abdominal fat, and effects are unlikely to be clinically meaningful for most people.

- A 2023 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis in the *British Journal of Nutrition* found CLA supplementation caused only small, statistically significant improvements in body composition (body mass, BMI, waist circumference), but "data from high-quality studies failed to show CLA's body fat-lowering properties," and effect sizes were unlikely to be clinically important ([Cambridge Core](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366)).

- An earlier meta-analysis (Whigham et al., *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition*, 2007) reported a modest average fat loss (~0.05 kg/week) but noted highly inconsistent human results compared to strong animal data ([AJCN](https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext)).

- Some individual RCTs specifically targeting abdominal fat showed positive results: a small trial in obese men with metabolic syndrome found CLA reduced abdominal adipose tissue over 4 weeks, though without broader metabolic benefits and needing larger confirmation ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11477497/)). A 2020 RCT in overweight/obese women also found reductions in visceral, android, and gynoid fat over 12 weeks ([MDPI](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/12/6/1811)).

**Bottom line:** CLA may cause a slight reduction in abdominal/visceral fat in some populations, but evidence is mixed, effect sizes are small, and higher-quality studies show weaker or null effects. It should not be considered a reliable or potent fat-loss supplement.
